# Swimlane process map

An ordered sequence of process steps, each assigned to the role, department, or system responsible — showing exactly where the process hands off from one lane to another, and honestly flagging any step nobody's actually named as owning.

Family: Problem definition · Format: .xlsx · Domain: core

## What it is

A swimlane process map is the process laid out as an ordered sequence of steps, each assigned to the lane — the role, department, or system — responsible for it. Reading down the lane column shows exactly where the process hands off from one owner to another; reading the sequence shows the real order things happen in. It's deliberately linear, not a branching flowchart — the primary path, captured honestly, is more useful here than an attempt to diagram every exception. A step with no lane assigned is a real finding: nobody's actually accountable for it, whether or not the process still somehow gets through it.

## When to use it

Use it when:

- You're mapping a process that crosses multiple roles or departments and want to see exactly where the handoffs happen.
- You suspect ownership is unclear somewhere in the process and want an honest record of which steps actually have a named owner.
- You're scoping a Transactional Process Improvement (TPI) review and need to see the process's real shape before deciding where to focus.

Not when:

- The process runs entirely within one role or team with no real handoffs — a work instruction fits a single-owner process better than a tool built to show cross-lane movement.
- You need to model branches, exceptions, or decision points in detail — this tool captures the primary path only; note a real deviation in a step's own note field rather than trying to diagram every branch.
- You want to skip actually walking the process and just guess at the lanes — an assigned-but-wrong lane is worse than an honestly empty one, since it looks resolved when it isn't.

## How to fill it in

- **steps** — Describe the process roughly, in order — a first-pass step sequence with a lane for each gets built from that, for you to correct against the real process and real ownership.
- **coverage** — Computed for you from your steps and their lanes — nothing to enter here.
- **narrative** — Drafted from the map actually built.
- **nextSteps** — What will you do about an unassigned step or a heavy handoff count, ranked by impact and effort, owned and dated.

## What good looks like

The example below maps the same Meridian Business Services vendor invoice approval process the eight wastes worksheet walks — eight steps across four lanes, four real handoffs, and one step, releasing payment to the vendor, honestly left with no named owner because nobody in the process as described is actually accountable for confirming it happened correctly.

Full worked example, on-screen and as a downloadable .xlsx: https://www.katafacts.com/katas/swimlane-process-map

## Common mistakes

- **Assigning a plausible-sounding lane to a step nobody's actually confirmed owns it.** — A wrongly-assigned lane looks resolved on the map but isn't — the whole value of an honestly empty lane is that it's visibly still a gap.
- **Trying to model every exception and branch instead of the primary path.** — A map cluttered with every edge case is harder to read than a clean primary path with real deviations noted separately — the vital few discipline applies to process mapping too.
- **Building the map once and never re-checking it as the process actually changes.** — A swimlane map is only as good as how current it is — a step's real owner can quietly change without anyone updating the map.

## What it connects to

Upstream:

- **Eight wastes (DOWNTIME) worksheet** — A waste walk's findings often reveal exactly which lane or handoff is worth mapping in detail next — the two tools examine the same process from different angles.

Downstream:

- **Kaizen event charter** — An unassigned step or a heavy handoff cluster found here is exactly the kind of concrete finding that justifies chartering a real kaizen event.
- **Work instruction** — Once a step's real owner is confirmed, a work instruction is where that lane's actual procedure gets standardized.

## Where AI helps

Judgement — stays with you:

- Deciding whether a step genuinely has no owner or the description just didn't say
- Deciding which handoff or unassigned step to chase down first

Analysis — AI helps:

- Drafting a first-pass step sequence and lane assignment from a description of the process
- Drafting the narrative from the map actually built

Drudgery — automated:

- Computing lane count, handoff count, and steps per lane
- Flagging every step with no lane assigned
- Exporting to xlsx in the house format
